topics.title: Māui and Mahuika: The Secret of Fire
facts: Māui visits his ancestress Mahuika seeking fire.
In this telling, Mahuika gives him fire from her burning fingernails.
He repeatedly extinguishes the fire and returns asking for more.
Mahuika grows angry after she realizes she has been tricked.
Fire spreads through a forest and Māui flees.
Rain and water help end the danger in some tellings.
Fire remains in the trees used to create fire by friction.

topics.title: Rūaumoko: The Earth Beneath Our Feet

sources.title: Te Ara — Earthquakes in Māori tradition

facts: One traditional account describes Rūaumoko as a child of Ranginui and Papatūānuku.
After their separation, the children turn their grieving mother Papatūānuku over.
Rūaumoko remains with his mother beneath the earth.
He is associated with earthquakes and volcanic activity.
The trembling land is explained in this tradition through his movements.

topics.title: Rātā and the Tree That Returned

sources.title: Te Ara — Māori relationship with the forest (Rātā tradition)
New Zealand Curriculum — Rātā me te Rākau

facts: Rātā enters the forest seeking a tree to make a waka.
He fells a tree and begins preparing it for the canoe.
When he returns, the tree is standing upright again.
He cuts it again and is puzzled to find it restored.
The hākuturi, guardians of the forest in the form of living creatures, restore the tree.
Rātā learns that he did not follow the appropriate tikanga respecting the forest.
In one telling, after he pays respect the forest guardians allow him to use the tree.
The story is remembered as teaching respect and care for the natural world.

topics.title: Tāne and the Three Baskets of Knowledge

sources.title: Te Ara — Ranginui as knowledge and life
Te Ara — Education in traditional Māori society

facts: One tradition describes Tāne journeying through the heavens in search of knowledge.
Tāne ascends towards the highest of the twelve heavens.
In one account the destination is Te Tihi-o-Manono at Te Toi-o-ngā-rangi.
He retrieves three baskets of knowledge, known as kete wānanga.
Their names include te kete-tuatea, te kete-tuauri and te kete-aronui.
Interpretations of the three baskets vary in Māori scholarship and across traditions.
The tale links knowledge, learning and the origins of life with Ranginui and Tāne.
